profile.reading:
Per Flexential's own individual facility page, this building (Flexential Las Vegas - Downtown) is located at 304 East Carson Avenue, Suite 370, Las Vegas, NV 89101. The operator publishes a footprint of 33135 square feet and 1.37 MW of critical load UPS capacity for this specific building, with published certifications and compliance attestations including PCI DSS, SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, HITRUST CSF, NIST 800-53, ITAR, SSAE 18. Nevada launched its data center sales- and property-tax abatement program in 2015 as a post-recession economic development tool; a Nevada Independent analysis found the state had approved $457 million in combined projected tax abatements over the following decade (15 abatements, 2 later withdrawn) and that local governments missed out on more than $537 million in sales and use tax revenue over eight years, while the abated projects promised roughly 300 permanent jobs, or about $1.5 million in incentive per job, far above the roughly $190,000 per job Nevada offered Tesla for 6,500 positions. A 2023 analysis found Nevada's data center sector overall, including non-abated facilities, employed 4,550 people and generated $290 million in state and local tax revenue. Storey County, east of Reno, hosts more than half of the state's abated data centers, including Google and Switch facilities, a different submarket from Flexential's Las Vegas-area buildings. Union electrical workers reported heavy construction activity tied to data centers, with one Northern Nevada local reporting 4,000 electricians deployed, about 80% on data center projects.

Clark County, home to both Las Vegas Flexential buildings, is a distinct jurisdiction from the Storey County tax-abatement submarket near Reno and has its own active 2026 data center policy debate. Switch operates 11 data centers spanning more than 2 million square feet in the Las Vegas area; Clark County commissioners approved a roughly 57,000-square-foot expansion of an existing Switch facility in southwest Las Vegas on June 17, 2026, after opposition from Sierra Club members and area residents, and on July 7, 2026 directed staff to study new land-use and environmental standards for data centers amid growing calls for regulation, according to the Nevada Independent and Las Vegas Review-Journal. Separately, Google's Henderson data center consumed more than 404 million gallons of water for cooling in 2024, non-recoverable water converted to mist, even after the Southern Nevada Water Authority banned evaporative cooling in new commercial buildings in 2023 (Google's facility was grandfathered in); data centers accounted for about 22% of Nevada's electricity consumption in 2024, with NV Energy projecting statewide data center load could reach 64% of the utility's electricity sales by 2046, per FOX5 Las Vegas investigative reporting.

reading.body:
At 1.37 MW of published IT capacity across 33,135 square feet, this facility is too small for large-model AI training, which routinely consumes tens or hundreds of megawatts in a single cluster.

The power-to-space ratio suggests either modest-scale inference or enterprise colocation. Assuming 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 1.37 MW supports roughly 34 racks. At the lower inference density of 10 kW per rack, the same power reaches roughly 137 racks. Neither scenario matches the concentrated compute buildout that AI scaling requires.

The certification stack makes the intended workload explicit. SOC 1 Type II and SOC 2 Type II qualify the facility for audited financial controls. PCI DSS qualifies it for payment-card processing. ITAR qualifies it for defense and export-controlled data. HITRUST qualifies it for regulated healthcare. NIST 800-53 qualifies it for federal security frameworks. These certifications point toward compliance-sensitive enterprise workloads, not the high-density compute clusters that AI development depends on.

Within Nevada, this site ranks second by published capacity among facilities with a megawatt figure reported here, out of 26 mapped facilities in the state. The certification profile and power footprint suggest this facility serves regulated enterprise customers rather than the AI infrastructure buildout now concentrating in purpose-built hyperscale data centers elsewhere.
